title: Maritime Psychology: Definition, Scope and Conceptualization

findings.antecedent: Maritime environment
findings.consequent: People's perception of opportunities and threats
findings.quote: The maritime environment is vast and clearly there are differences in how people perceive both opportunities and threats within their own experience of an environment (Walsh-Danishmandi and MacLachlan 2000).

findings.antecedent: Larger ships, greater mechanization, and reduced manning levels in seafaring
findings.consequent: Seafarer experience, outlets for affiliation, collective identity, individual worth, support, and mental well-being
findings.quote: With larger ships, greater mechanization and reduced manning levels, more is required from seafarers and there are fewer outlets for the sort of affiliation that sustains both a sense of collective identity and individual worth and support.

findings.antecedent: Individual psychological interventions in a fundamentally unfair and exploitative working environment
findings.quote: So no matter what sort of clever individual psychological interventions maritime psychologists can develop, implementing these in a fundamentally unfair and exploitive working environment can be counterproductive, individualizing a sys tems problem (McVeigh et al. 2016).

findings.antecedent: Unfair and exploitative working practices (e.g., 'sweat ships', FOC ships, long hours, power imbalance)
findings.consequent: Psychological well-being, rights of individuals, organizational justice, and decency in the workplace
findings.quote: These practices, therefore, affect not only the psychological well-being and rights of individuals, but also the sense of organizational justice and expectations for decency that pervade the workplace (MacLachlan 2016).

findings.antecedent: Diminishing communal living space on board merchant ships
findings.quote: the space allocated to communal living on board merchant ships has been diminishing in recent times (Sampson 2015): the design of living space on board will reflect the legislative environment and the attitude of the company towards social spaces; the use of such space will reflect the sense of teamwork and con geniality on board—and the existence of such an atmosphere will in turn reflect the demand for such space to be built into ships at the design stage.

findings.antecedent: Modelling simulations of evacuation scenarios (considering door sizes, number of doors/passengers, ship heel/trim angles)
findings.consequent: Bottlenecks in ship layout and evacuation time
findings.quote: Yuan et al. (2014) illustrate, using a neighbourhood particle swarm optimization model, how door sizes, the number of doors, the number of passengers, along with the ship’s heel and trim angles, all affect the evacuation time of a given ship design.

findings.antecedent: Majority of elderly passengers on cruise ships
findings.quote: With the majority of passengers on some cruise ships being elderly, it seems likely that the evacuation scenarios and times for these passengers are going to be more complex and take longer than for younger or less impaired passengers.

findings.antecedent: Seafarers attacked or held hostage by pirates
findings.consequent: Concerns about returning to work, sleep disturbances, diminished energy, increased alcohol use, loss of pleasure, irritability, and suicidal thoughts
findings.quote: The Centre for Seafarers’ Rights, of the Seamen’s Church Institute, conducted a study of 25 seafarers attacked or held hostage by pirates (Stevenson 2012), which found that most had concerns about returning to work (20), sleep disturbances (12) and diminished energy (10). Some of them also reported increased use of alcohol (7), loss of pleasure from what had been formerly pleasurable activities (6), with fewer reporting a deterioration of significant relationships (5), irritability (5) and sometimes thoughts of suicide (3).

findings.antecedent: Longer time held captive by pirates
findings.consequent: Severity of symptoms (detachment, alienation, startled by noises, nightmares, sleep disturbance, anxiety, tension, fear, low mood, lack of interest/engagement)
findings.quote: Within this small sample there was no relationship between subjective descriptions of stress, and age, rank or length of service at sea, but there was a relationship with the length of time seafarers were held captive—the longer they were held, the more severe the symptoms.

findings.antecedent: Stigma associated with mental health problems in seafarers
findings.quote: Furthermore, they argue; “Stigma discourages many seafarers from seeking consultation or effective therapy … because they fear losing their jobs or not being rehired” (p. 993).

findings.antecedent: Democratic command styles
findings.quote: O’Shea (2005) has demonstrated that certain styles of command—generally more democratic styles—are associated with better sea farer well-being.

findings.antecedent: Work Improvement on Board (WIB) programmes with participatory action-oriented training (applied flexibly)
findings.consequent: Benefits in the Japanese fishing fleet
findings.quote: Researching the effects of Work Improvement on Board (WIB) programmes in the Japanese fishing fleet, Shuji and Kazutaka (2015), using participatory action-orientated training, found such interventions to be beneficial, especially when applied in a flexible manner.

findings.antecedent: Cultivating pluralism (diversity of views) in organizational culture
findings.quote: Organizational culture should also cultivate pluralism (MacLachlan and O’Connell 2000) as a diversity of views in the workplace can in fact help solve problems and does not need to be a challenge to one narrow prevailing ethos (Cox and Blake 1991).

findings.antecedent: Psychological Capital (PsyCap)
findings.consequent: Organizational effectiveness and positive work outcomes
findings.quote: This motivational state has been shown to be related to organizational effectiveness and positive work outcomes (Newman et al. 2014), and has recently been explored in the maritime environment by Bergheim et al. (2015).

findings.antecedent: Psychological Capital (PsyCap)
findings.quote: Their first study found that PsyCap was positively associated with per ceptions of safety climate and importantly this effect still held after controlling for socially desirable responding.

findings.antecedent: High levels of PsyCap in officers (compared to non-officers with high PsyCap)
findings.quote: for officers and non-officers who scored relatively low on PsyCap, they perceived the safety climate similarly; however, officers with high levels of PsyCap had a more positive perception of the safety climate, compared to non-officers who also scored high on PsyCap.

findings.antecedent: PsyCap's relationship to safety climate
findings.quote: In a second study they demonstrated that PsyCap’s relationship to safety climate was mediated by its association with job satisfaction.

findings.antecedent: High PsyCap and greater job satisfaction
findings.quote: those with high scores on psychological capital felt their ship was safer, at least in part, due to them also having greater job satisfaction.

findings.antecedent: Positive emotions
findings.quote: accumulating evidence is providing empirical support for such folk theories... positive emotions are associated with beneficial psychological and physical health effects; positive emotions can be an important factor that safeguards individuals against maladaptive health outcomes (Tugade et al. 2004).

findings.antecedent: Navigating painful emotions
findings.consequent: Happiness and reevaluation of one's life
findings.quote: navigating these painful emotions can contribute to increased happiness and possibly reevaluation of one’s life (MacLachlan and Hand 2013).

findings.antecedent: Relationships with other people
findings.quote: Relationships, our key to the “connected life,” are therefore a cornerstone of flourishing as proposed by Seligman’s theory of well-being. As declared by Seligman, relationships with other people may be the most effective antidote to the “downs” of life and the single most dependable “up” (Seligman 2011b).

findings.antecedent: Cultivating relationships, partaking in absorbing work/leisure, and cultivating an optimistic perspective
findings.quote: scientific research indi cates three reliable ways to promote happiness: (1) cultivate relationships that comprise deep attachment and commitment; (2) partake in absorbing work and leisure activities in which you avail of your strengths, talents and interests; and (3) cultivate an optimistic, future-oriented perspective on life in which you expect the best to happen (Carr 2011).

findings.antecedent: Positive psychology interventions
findings.consequent: Components of the 'good life' (positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, accomplishment)
findings.quote: A growing literature on such positive psychology interventions indicates that the “good life”—positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accom plishment—can be strengthened (Seligman 2010).

findings.antecedent: Positive psychology interventions
findings.consequent: Subjective and psychological well-being, depressive symptoms
findings.quote: in a meta-analytical study of the effectiveness of positive psychology interventions, Bolier and colleagues reported that positive psychology interventions significantly enhanced subjective and psychological well-being and reduced depressive symp toms (Bolier et al. 2013).

findings.antecedent: 'Three good things' and 'using signature strengths' interventions
findings.quote: Seligman et al. found that two interventions—writing about three good things that happened each day and why they happened, and using signature strengths of character in a new way—made people happier (and less depressed) up to 6 months later (Seligman et al. 2005).

findings.antecedent: Diverse interventions (finding positive meaning, relaxation training, invoking empathy or amusement)
findings.quote: As emphasized by Fredrickson, diverse interventions—including finding positive meaning, relaxation training, and invok ing empathy or amusement—share the capacity to evoke positive emotions while lessening negative emotions (Fredrickson 2000).

findings.antecedent: Overvaluing happiness (with high expectations)
findings.quote: The researchers propose that valuing happiness may lead people to feel less happy in positive contexts when expectations for happiness are high (Mauss et al. 2011).

findings.antecedent: Promoting well-being by directing efforts on specific activities (e.g., acts of kindness)
findings.quote: Accordingly, activities to promote well-being may be more effective when aimed to direct participants’ efforts on the specific activity, such as practicing acts of kindness, rather than on the sole value of increasing happiness (Nelson and Lyubomirsky 2012).

findings.antecedent: Progress towards motive-congruent goals
findings.quote: In a study conducted by Brunstein et al. (1998), the researchers found that progress towards motive-congruent goals, in contrast to progress towards motive-incongruent goals, accounted for a sample of students’ daily experiences of emotional well-being.

findings.antecedent: Positive self-statement ('I’m a lovable person') among participants with low self-esteem
findings.quote: among participants with low self-esteem, those who repeated a positive self-statement (“I’m a lovable person”) felt worse than those with low self-esteem who did not repeat the statement

findings.antecedent: Gender
findings.consequent: Self-reported person-activity fit for PP interventions (gratitude journal, acts of kindness, savouring life’s joys)
findings.quote: Thompson and colleagues investigated how gender may affect self-reported person-activity fit across three positive psychology interventions: gratitude journal; acts of kindness; and savouring life’s joys. The results indicated that gender influenced person-activity fit regarding the above interventions, with females in all cases reporting a higher fit than males (Thompson et al. 2014).

findings.antecedent: Employees’ positive psychological resource capacities (hope, optimism, resilience)
findings.consequent: Work-related employee outcomes (performance, job satisfaction, work happiness, organizational commitment)
findings.quote: Their findings generally supported their hypotheses that employees’ positive psycho logical resource capacities related to, and contributed equal variance to, the out comes (Youssef and Luthans 2007).

findings.antecedent: Positive speech among team members
findings.consequent: Performance in business teams (profitability, customer satisfaction, assessments)
findings.quote: Findings indicated that high-performance teams showed more positive speech, providing empirical support for positive speech among team members as distin guishing high-performance teams from less successfully performing teams (Losada 1999).

findings.antecedent: Psychological capital
findings.quote: From a sample of seafarers working on oil platform supply ships, empirical support is provided by Hystad et al. for psychological capital as an important factor of safety climate (Hystad et al. 2014).

findings.antecedent: Psychological capital (including resiliency)
findings.consequent: Perceptions of safety climate among maritime workers
findings.quote: Bergheim et al. reported that psychological capital, including resiliency, was pos itively associated with perceptions of safety climate (Bergheim et al. 2015).

findings.antecedent: Psychological resilience
findings.quote: Research shows that resilience has a positive relationship with recovery from daily stressors. Ong et al. found that psychological resilience accounted for meaningful differences in emotional responses to daily stressors.

findings.antecedent: Positive emotions
findings.consequent: High-resilient individuals' capacity to recover effectively from daily stress
findings.quote: Their findings indicated that, over time, the experience of positive emotions may function to assist high-resilient individuals in their capacity to recover effectively from daily stress (Ong et al. 2006).

findings.antecedent: Positive emotions
findings.consequent: Enduring personal resources (physical, intellectual, social, psychological)
findings.quote: The Broaden-and-Build theory (Fredrickson 2001) postulates that experiences of positive emotions serve to build enduring personal resources—including physical, intellectual, social and psycho logical resources—and are a resource that can be used when individuals undergo stressful experiences.

findings.antecedent: Effectively employed positive emotions
findings.consequent: Psychological resilience, health, and subjective well-being
findings.quote: As proposed by Fredrickson, positive emotions, when effectively employed, can optimize psychological resilience, health, and subjective well-being (Fredrickson 2000).

findings.antecedent: Positive emotions and resilience
findings.quote: Positive emotions boost resilience, which in turn stimulates more positive feelings; in other words, positive emotions and resilience mutually reinforce each other (Smith and Hollinger-Smith 2015).

findings.antecedent: Hardy leaders communicating a positive construction of shared stressful experiences
findings.consequent: Group's positive interpretation of the experience
findings.quote: It is through this “shaping” of stressful experiences that leaders may foster hardy-resilient response patterns in a group setting, whereby a leader high in hardiness communicates a positive construction of shared stressful expe riences, which may influence the entire group in the direction of a more positive interpretation of the experience (Bartone 2010, 2012).

findings.antecedent: Resilience training programmes
findings.consequent: Health, well-being, and quality of life
findings.quote: Accordingly, training programmes that aim to develop or enhance resilience may be effective in improving health, well-being and quality of life (Leppin et al. 2014).

findings.antecedent: Strengths and positive health aspects focused interview model (compared to traditional medical diagnostic interview)
findings.consequent: Post-assessment referrals for counselling and later distress
findings.quote: a significant difference was found in relation to post-assessment referrals for counselling, suggesting that this innovative positive psychology interview approach may have contributed to preventing later distress (van Wijk and Waters 2008).

findings.antecedent: Positive psychology interventions like 'Three good things in life' for seafarers
findings.quote: Positive psychology interventions such as “Three good things in life” for seafarers may facilitate increases in happiness and decreases in depressive symptoms for up to 6 months

findings.antecedent: Computer-based training for seafarers (on board and on shore) for psychological capital
findings.consequent: Psychological capital and well-being of seafarers
findings.quote: Computer-based training for seafarers on board and on shore may provide an effective approach for programmes aiming to enhance psychological capital and well-being of seafarers on a wider and cost-effective scale

findings.antecedent: Mindfulness meditation training for maritime workers
findings.consequent: Cognitive capacity, sustained attention, performance, and safety in maritime organizations
findings.quote: Mindfulness meditation training may enhance cognitive capacity of maritime workers, such as improved sustained attention, the effect of which may be enhanced performance and safety in maritime organizations

findings.antecedent: Writing about life goals for maritime workers
findings.quote: Writing about life goals may generate health benefits for maritime workers such as increased subjective well-being and decreased illness.

findings.antecedent: Identifying and using one’s signature strengths for maritime workers
findings.quote: Positive psychology interventions such as identifying and using one’s signature strengths may be an effective approach to increasing happiness and decreasing depressive symptoms of maritime workers

findings.antecedent: Psychologically focused skills and regular psychological monitoring for mariners
findings.consequent: Psychological resilience, early problem detection, and timely support
findings.quote: Equipping mariners with the right psychologically focused skills and regular psychological monitoring can be effective methods of improving psychological resilience, detecting problems at an early stage, ensuring timely support and where necessary signposting to evidence based medical interventions” (March on Stress 2013).

findings.antecedent: Mindfulness
findings.quote: Mindfulness... has been shown to increase positive affect and decrease negative affect (Davis and Hayes 2012).

findings.antecedent: Mindfulness-Based Mind Fitness Training (MMFT)
findings.consequent: Enhanced recovery and altered stress recovery mechanisms
findings.quote: marines who received Mindfulness-Based Mind Fitness Training (MMFT) showed inter alia enhanced recovery including heart rate and breathing rate after stressful training, signifying that mechanisms relating to stress recovery can be altered in healthy individuals prior to stress exposure (Johnson et al. 2014).

findings.antecedent: MMFT practice
findings.quote: marines who engaged more in MMFT practice showed greater self-reported mindfulness, associated with decreases in perceived stress (Stanley et al. 2011).

findings.antecedent: Online or computer-based positive psychology interventions
findings.consequent: People's ability to manage well-being, accessibility, cost, and scalability
findings.quote: Online positive psychology interventions have the capacity to empower people to manage their own well-being, while being highly accessible, low-cost, and scalable, reaching diverse types of populations (Bolier et al. 2014; Drozd et al. 2014; Redzic et al. 2014).

findings.antecedent: Web-based training intervention to develop psychological capital
findings.quote: Luthans et al. found that the treatment group in a web-based training intervention to develop positive psychological capital, but not the control group, experienced a significant increase in their psychological capital (Luthans et al. 2008).

findings.antecedent: Shipping companies investing in seafarer well-being
findings.quote: shipping companies are seemingly willing to invest in the well-being of seafarers as it is considered a primary source of productivity (Progoulaki et al. 2013).
